entries.name: Gregory the Great
entries.statusDescription: Not counted as a candidate tradition of its own — its story is told plainly inside another tradition's, rather than standing alone.
entries.sourcing: Rich. The Library holds ten of his own works on the shelf of the Roman church of his age. They include the Pastoral Rule, the Moralia on Job, the Dialogues, and his letters in English and in Latin.
entries.relationsSummary: Gregory is told within The Roman Church in the Age of Gregory the Great, the entry named for his years as bishop. Where he wrote to other churches or sent men to them, that entry's links name him.
entries.why: Gregory was a monk first. Then he was the pope's envoy at Constantinople, and from 590 the bishop of Rome. Between those duties he wrote books the Latin West read for centuries. Among them are the Pastoral Rule, the Moralia on Job and the Dialogues.
entries.teaser: Rome and Constantinople, c. 578 to 604. A monk made bishop against his will in a city struck by plague, who kept writing while he governed it.
entries.longDescription:
Gregory came from a Roman family of rank. When his father died, he kept only a small part of what he inherited. He founded six monasteries in Sicily, and a seventh in his own house on the Caelian hill in Rome. He entered that one as a monk, and later became its abbot.

He was not left there long. The pope made him a deacon and sent him to Constantinople as his envoy, probably from 578 to 585. There he met Leander, bishop of Seville. At Leander's urging he began the Moralia, a long commentary on the Book of Job.

In 590 Pope Pelagius II died of the disease then raging in Rome, and the clergy and people chose Gregory to follow him. He did not want the office. His biographers say he wrote to the emperor and begged him not to confirm the choice. He was ordained on 3 September 590.

His pen did not stop while he governed. The Pastoral Rule teaches bishops how to govern souls, which it calls the art of arts. The Dialogues gather the lives and miracles of the saints of Italy, Benedict among them. In his last months gout left him at times hardly able to speak, yet he still wrote letters. He died on 12 March 604.
voices: Gregory the Great — monk, papal envoy at Constantinople, and from 590 bishop of Rome, whose own books and letters survive
Leander of Seville - his friend from the Constantinople years, at whose urging he began the Moralia
entries.legacy: His Pastoral Rule outlived him by centuries. A Carolingian list told canons to know 'the pastoral book', and King Alfred had it put into English to send to every bishop in his kingdom. His Dialogues hold the only life of Benedict there is. Everything he did as bishop of Rome is told in the entry for his church.

entries.name: William Tyndale
entries.region: England, then Cologne, Worms and Antwerp
entries.statusDescription: Not counted as a candidate tradition of its own — its story is told plainly inside another tradition's, rather than standing alone.
entries.sourcing: Good, for one man. The Library holds two volumes of his own writing, shelved with the English Reformation as its forerunner. They hold his treatises and the prologues to his Bible, with Foxe's account of his life and death.
entries.relationsSummary: Tyndale is told within the English Reformation, as its forerunner. His work came before that reform's start in the 1530s, and his use of Luther is carried on the Wittenberg link.
entries.why: William Tyndale put the New Testament into English and printed it abroad. It was in the press by 1525, years before Henry VIII broke with Rome in the 1530s. So he stands before the English Reformation, as its forerunner, and died at the stake in 1536.
entries.teaser: Worms and Antwerp, 1525 to 1536. An English scholar in exile who wanted a ploughboy to know the Scriptures, and died at the stake for his books.
entries.longDescription:
Tyndale was born near the Welsh border and studied at Oxford, then at Cambridge. John Foxe tells of a quarrel with a learned priest. Tyndale said that, if God spared his life, he would make a boy who drives the plough know more of the Scripture than the priest did.

He went abroad to print his New Testament. It was in the press at Cologne in 1525, until an enemy of Luther found out the work. Tyndale moved to Worms and printed it there. A report of 1526 said six thousand copies had been printed.

Copies were smuggled into England. In February 1526 Cardinal Wolsey watched baskets of books burn at St Paul's in London. Tyndale said copies of his own book were among them.

He kept writing in exile. The Obedience of a Christian Man came out in 1528, and in 1530 he printed his version of the five books of Moses. In 1535 an Englishman named Henry Philips won his trust at Antwerp. Philips pointed him out to the officers who seized him.

He was condemned under the emperor's decree. At Vilvoorde in 1536 he was strangled at the stake, and his body was burned. Foxe gives his last words: 'Lord, open the king of England's eyes.'
voices: William Tyndale — translator and writer in exile, whose treatises and prologues the Library holds
John Foxe - the martyrologist whose Acts and Monuments keep the story of his life and death
entries.legacy: Before the year of his death was out, the king's own printer issued Tyndale's New Testament in England. His name was printed on its title page. Much of his Prologue to Romans comes from Luther's own preface, so England's debt to Wittenberg runs through him. The reform he did not live to see is told in the English Reformation's own entry.

entries.name: Thomas à Kempis
entries.region: Mount St Agnes near Zwolle, and Deventer
entries.statusDescription: Not counted as a candidate tradition of its own — its story is told plainly inside another tradition's, rather than standing alone.
entries.sourcing: Rich. The Library holds fourteen of his own works on the Devotio Moderna shelf. They include his chronicle, his lives of the founders and his sermons, with the Imitation credited to him.
entries.relationsSummary: Thomas is told within the Devotio Moderna. That movement formed him. The Imitation's reach to the Jesuits is shown on the movement's own link.
entries.why: Thomas was made a canon of Mount St Agnes near Zwolle in 1406, and he stayed in that small house until he died in 1471. He copied books, wrote its chronicle and the lives of the movement's founders, and wrote little books for the young. The Imitation of Christ is credited to him, though that has long been disputed.
entries.teaser: Mount St Agnes, 1406 to 1471. A canon who copied books in one small house all his life, and who is credited with the most copied Christian book after the Bible.
entries.longDescription:
Thomas Hemerken was born in the town of Kempen, in the diocese of Cologne, and his name means 'of Kempen'. As a youth he heard Florentius Radewijns at Deventer. When Thomas was twenty, Florentius sent him to the new house of Mount St Agnes. Its prior was Thomas's own brother, John of Kempen.

He was invested as a canon there in 1406, after six years of probation. He stayed for the rest of his life, and for a time served as sub-prior. He copied a whole Bible for the house, and many other books for its use and for sale.

He also wrote. His chronicle records Mount St Agnes year by year. His lives of Gerard Groote, Florentius and their followers keep the movement's memory of its founders. A brother of the house praised his little books for the young as plain in style but mighty in matter.

The Imitation of Christ is credited to him. Johannes Busch, a canon of Windesheim in Thomas's own day, names him as its author. An early English translator, William Atkynson, gave it to Jean Gerson of Paris instead. In 1886 William Benham, who put it into English, argued that Thomas had only copied it. The question is still argued.

He died in 1471, in his ninety-second year. He had been a priest for more than fifty-seven years.
voices: Thomas à Kempis — canon of Mount St Agnes, chronicler of his house and biographer of the movement's founders
Johannes Busch - canon of Windesheim, whose chronicle names Thomas as the author of the Imitation
An unnamed brother of Mount St Agnes - who carried Thomas's chronicle on past 1471 and wrote the notice of his death
entries.legacy: His lasting work is a book. The Imitation was read far beyond the houses, and Ignatius of Loyola kept it on his desk, as the Devotio Moderna's entry tells. His chronicle and lives remain an inside record of the movement's houses.

entries.name: John Wyclif
entries.statusDescription: Not counted as a candidate tradition of its own — its story is told plainly inside another tradition's, rather than standing alone.
entries.sourcing: Rich. The Library holds twelve of his own works on the Lollardy shelf, in Latin and in English. The Bible made by his circle stands beside them.
entries.relationsSummary: Wyclif is told within Lollardy, the movement that grew from his teaching. His pull on Jan Hus and the church's case against him are carried on Lollardy's links.
entries.why: John Wyclif spent most of his life as a scholar at Oxford, and his last years as parish priest of Lutterworth. His opinions were condemned by the pope in 1377 and by an English synod in 1382, yet he died free, in his own parish.
entries.teaser: Oxford and Lutterworth, c. 1360 to 1384. A scholar who took on the friars, the pope and the teaching of the Mass, and whose followers outlived him by more than a century.
entries.longDescription:
Wyclif, also spelled Wycliffe, made his name at Oxford. From about 1360 he argued there against the friars. His 1845 editor says Balliol College chose him as its head in the same years.

He also served the king. In 1374 he went to Bruges as one of the royal envoys, to protest against English church posts going to foreigners named by the pope. The crown then gave him the parish of Lutterworth in Leicestershire.

In June 1377 the pope sent letters to England against his opinions. In 1382 Archbishop Courtenay called a synod in London to judge them. As it met, an earthquake shook the city, and some there took it as a warning from Heaven. Courtenay read it the other way, and the synod went on.

His circle made the English Bible that bears his name. Its editors in 1850 thought the New Testament was probably his own work. They gave much of the Old Testament to his helper Nicholas Hereford.

On 29 December 1384, as he gave out the bread at Mass, he was struck by paralysis. He died two days later.
voices: John Wyclif — Oxford theologian and rector of Lutterworth, whose Latin and English works the Library holds
Nicholas Hereford - the helper to whom an early note gives much of the Old Testament in the English Bible of Wyclif's circle
entries.legacy: His books crossed Europe. In Prague, Jan Hus took paragraph after paragraph from Wyclif's book on the Church. In 1415 the Council of Constance condemned Wyclif's errors, more than thirty years after his death. In England his teaching grew into Lollardy, whose story is told in its own entry.

entries.name: Martin Luther
entries.statusDescription: Not counted as a candidate tradition of its own — its story is told plainly inside another tradition's, rather than standing alone.
entries.sourcing: Very rich. The Library holds forty-seven of his own works on the Wittenberg shelf. They include his treatises, catechisms and letters, and his Table Talk.
entries.relationsSummary: Luther is told within Lutheran Wittenberg and its congregations. That tradition grew from his protest of 1517. His quarrels and ties with other churches are shown on that entry's links.
entries.why: Martin Luther was a miner's son from Eisleben, and a friar who taught at Wittenberg. Before the emperor he would not take back his books, and he put the Bible into German.
entries.teaser: Wittenberg, 1517 to 1546. A friar and teacher whose letter against the sale of indulgences began a movement that still bears his name.
entries.longDescription:
Luther was born at Eisleben in 1483. His father was a poor miner. He became an Augustinian friar and taught theology at Wittenberg.

On 31 October 1517 he wrote to the archbishop of Mainz about the indulgences sold under the archbishop's name. His theses of the same day said the indulgence preachers were in error. A later story says he also nailed the theses to the castle church door. It comes from an account written after his death, and historians still disagree about it.

In June 1520 a papal bull condemned his teaching. In April 1521 he stood before the emperor Charles V at the Diet of Worms. He refused to take anything back unless Scripture showed him he was wrong. Then he was hidden at the Wartburg castle. There he began what an 1885 historian called the great work of his life, a German Bible from the original text.

He went on writing for twenty-five years more: sermons, hymns, letters, and in 1529 a Small and a Large Catechism. He died on 18 February 1546.
voices: Martin Luther — Augustinian friar and Wittenberg professor whose letter of 1517 began the movement told in Lutheran Wittenberg
Johann Aurifaber - Luther's disciple, who first gave his Table Talk to the world
entries.legacy: The Lutheran churches grew from his work, and their story is told in the Wittenberg entry and those after it. His Small Catechism is still learned by heart at home. His hymn tunes began a line of church music that runs to Bach. Many links across the tree concern him, from friends and foes alike.

entries.name: John Calvin
entries.statusDescription: Not counted as a candidate tradition of its own — its story is told plainly inside another tradition's, rather than standing alone.
entries.sourcing: Rich. The Library holds twelve of his own works on the shelf of the Reformed cities. They include the Institutes, his two books on Genesis, the Geneva catechism and three volumes of his letters.
entries.relationsSummary: Calvin is told within the Reformed cities of Zurich and Geneva. He did not found that tradition, which began under Zwingli at Zurich in 1519. His dealings with other churches are carried on its links.
entries.why: John Calvin came to Geneva in 1536. Zwingli had begun Zurich's reform seventeen years before, and the two men never met. He was a French exile, the author of the Institutes, and a pastor whose letters survive.
entries.teaser: Basel, Strasbourg and Geneva, 1536 to 1564. A French exile who hoped to live quietly as a scholar, and was held in Geneva to build its church.
entries.longDescription:
Calvin was born at Noyon in France in 1509. He studied law and theology at Paris, Orleans and Bourges. Persecution drove him out of France, and he went to the Swiss lands.

At Basel, as he later wrote, he was living 'retired and unknown'. There in 1536 he published the first known edition of the Institutes of the Christian Religion. Soon after, passing through Geneva, he was held there by William Farel and made one of its ministers.

His first years in Geneva ended in exile. He went to Strasbourg, where the second edition of the Institutes came out in 1539. In 1541 Geneva called him back, and his letters of that year show how much he dreaded the return.

The church order he then gave the city is told in the Reformed cities' entry. His own work went on in commentaries, letters and new editions of the Institutes. He hoped Michael Servetus would be sentenced to death, though he asked that the punishment be made less severe. In 1553 Geneva burned him. He died on 27 May 1564.
voices: John Calvin — French exile, author of the Institutes and pastor at Geneva, whose Institutes, commentaries and letters survive
William Farel - the Genevan preacher who held him in the city in 1536
entries.legacy: The Reformed churches that grew from Zurich and Geneva are told in their own entries. His name became a label for that whole family. In 1672 a synod of the Greek church met at Jerusalem 'against the Calvinists'. A Dutch teacher at Utrecht, asked if his church held Calvin's views, said yes, but Calvin was not its head.

entries.name: Ignatius of Loyola
entries.region: Loyola and Manresa, then Paris and Rome
entries.statusDescription: Not counted as a candidate tradition of its own — its story is told plainly inside another tradition's, rather than standing alone.
entries.sourcing: Rich. The Library holds ten of his own works on the Jesuit shelf. They include the life he dictated, the Spiritual Exercises and his letters.
entries.relationsSummary: Ignatius is told within the Society of Jesus, the order that grew from him and his companions. His men at Trent and his debt to the Imitation of Christ are carried on its links.
entries.why: Ignatius was a soldier, a beggar, a pilgrim and a student before he founded anything. He told his own story late, dictating it to a younger Jesuit between 1553 and 1555.
entries.teaser: Pamplona to Rome, 1521 to 1556. A wounded soldier who read the lives of the saints on his sickbed, begged his way to Jerusalem, and ended in Rome at the head of a new order.
entries.longDescription:
Ignatius was born in 1491 at the castle of Loyola, and grew up a page and then a soldier. At the siege of Pamplona a cannon ball broke one of his legs. In his slow recovery he read the lives of Christ and the saints, because the house had no other books.

He set out as a pilgrim. At Manresa he lived on the alms he begged each day. He reached Jerusalem, but he could not stay there. So he went back to school, to be better fitted to help souls.

At Paris he took his master's degree in March 1534. Francis Xavier and Peter Faber were his fellow students there. He and his companions meant to spend their lives in Jerusalem. If they could not, they would offer themselves to the pope.

No ship could take them, so they went to Rome. In 1540 Pope Paul III approved their Society. From Rome Ignatius sent out letters and instructions, among them orders for his men at the Council of Trent in 1546. He died on 31 July 1556.
voices: Ignatius of Loyola — soldier, pilgrim and founder, whose Spiritual Exercises, letters and dictated life survive
Luis Gonzalez da Camara - the younger Jesuit who took down his life story from 1553 to 1555
entries.legacy: The Society of Jesus is his lasting work, and its story is told in its own entry. His Spiritual Exercises shaped everyone the order trained. His dictated life is still the main record of how he changed.

entries.name: John Wesley
entries.statusDescription: Not counted as a candidate tradition of its own — its story is told plainly inside another tradition's, rather than standing alone.
entries.sourcing: Rich. The Library holds sixteen of his own works on the Methodist shelf. They include his journal in eight volumes, his sermons and his tracts.
entries.relationsSummary: Wesley is told within the Methodist revival, which grew from his preaching and his societies. What he took from Moravians, Pietists, Puritans and Luther is carried on its links.
entries.why: John Wesley kept a journal for fifty-five years, from his voyage to Georgia in 1735 until October 1790. It shows a priest who preached in the open air and looked on all the world as his parish.
entries.teaser: England and Georgia, 1735 to 1791. An Oxford priest whose heart was 'strangely warmed', who took the gospel into the fields and called the world his parish.
entries.longDescription:
John Wesley was a priest of the Church of England, trained at Oxford. In 1735 he sailed for the colony of Georgia. He wrote that he went not to escape want, nor to gain riches or honour, but to save his soul. The mission did not go well, as the revival's entry tells.

Back in London, in March 1738, the Moravian Peter Böhler convinced him that he lacked saving faith. On 24 May he went, unwillingly, to a meeting in Aldersgate Street, where someone was reading Luther's preface to Romans. There, he wrote, 'I felt my heart strangely warmed.' He now trusted in Christ alone for his salvation.

Many pulpits were closed to him. On 2 April 1739, at Bristol, he 'submitted to be more vile' and preached in the open air. Told that he had no right to preach in other men's parishes, he answered that he had none of his own. 'I look upon all the world as my parish,' he wrote.

He gathered his hearers into societies, and the revival's entry tells what they became. He read widely and judged for himself. In 1741 he read Luther's book on Galatians and called it shallow and confused. He kept his journal until October 1790, and died in 1791.
voices: John Wesley — priest, preacher and organizer, whose journal runs from 1735 to 1790
Peter Böhler - the Moravian who, by Wesley's own account, convinced him in 1738 that he lacked saving faith
entries.legacy: The Methodist churches grew from the societies he gathered, and their story runs on from the Methodist revival's entry. His journal records the revival from inside, day by day, for more than fifty years. He told his preachers to urge all believers to 'go on to perfection'. Holiness writers of the 1800s took up that teaching and called it his.

set.longDescription: It began with Geert Grote, a wealthy and worldly scholar of Deventer. He gave up his career and opened his own house to a group of devout women. Then he began preaching repentance in the towns of the IJssel valley. After his death in 1384 his followers organized. The Brothers and Sisters of the Common Life lived together and paid their way by copying books and other ordinary work. They took no vows and did not leave ordinary society. Beside them stood a stricter branch, the canons of Windesheim. Its houses kept their own chronicles. Johannes Busch wrote the chronicle of Windesheim, and Thomas à Kempis that of Mount St Agnes. What held them together was less a doctrine than a method: a plain, inward and orderly devotion. They had the habit of keeping a rapiarium, a personal notebook of gathered passages to return to. One such gathering became the Imitation of Christ. It is credited to Thomas à Kempis of Mount St Agnes near Zwolle, though its authorship is disputed. The houses also took in schoolboys and shaped the Latin schools of towns like Deventer and Zwolle. That is how the movement's way of shaping lives reached far more people than ever joined it.
set.why: Geert Grote gave up a rich career to gather devout men and women into shared homes. They lived in common without ever taking vows, and paid their way by copying books by hand. Each kept a private notebook of passages to return to, called a rapiarium. That habit produced the Imitation of Christ, the most copied Christian book after the Bible. It is credited to Thomas à Kempis, though its authorship is disputed. Their schools shaped Erasmus. Ignatius of Loyola, who founded the Jesuits, kept the Imitation on his desk. His Spiritual Exercises tell those who make them to read it.

set.note: Johannes Busch kept the chronicle of the Windesheim canons. He tells how their prior, at the council of Constance, gladly visited the cell of the friar who wrote the Clock of Eternal Wisdom. The chronicle's 1886 editor names that friar as Henry Suso. A 1902 editor of Thomas à Kempis lists Suso among the writers Thomas took sayings from.
